q: Which measure best expresses the probability that an individual animal will develop a disease over a defined period?
o: Cumulative incidence (incidence risk)
Point prevalence
Case fatality rate
e: Cumulative incidence is the proportion of an at-risk group that develops new disease over a stated period, which is the measure of individual risk. Prevalence reflects existing burden.

q: A shelter has widely varying lengths of stay. Why is the incidence rate, using animal-time at risk, often preferred to cumulative incidence?
o: It is easier to calculate by hand, because it uses fewer numbers.
It measures the existing burden of disease at one point in time.
The animal-time denominator accommodates unstable populations and varying follow-up.
e: Incidence rate uses total animal-time at risk, so it handles the variable follow-up created by differing lengths of stay.

q: When calculating the cumulative incidence of an in-shelter disease, which animals must be excluded from the at-risk denominator?
o: Animals housed individually rather than in groups
Animals already infected at the start of the period, and animals that arrive already infected
Animals that have been vaccinated
e: The denominator includes only animals capable of developing new disease, so existing and incoming cases are excluded.

q: A shelter tests every cat for FeLV on intake day and reports the proportion that is already infected. What is being measured?
o: Cumulative incidence
Point prevalence
Case fatality rate
e: Disease present at a single point in time in a population is point prevalence.

q: A disease has a chronic course of long duration. How will its prevalence compare with its incidence?
o: Prevalence will be low relative to incidence.
Prevalence and incidence will always be equal.
Prevalence will be high relative to incidence.
e: Prevalence is approximately incidence multiplied by average duration, so a long natural history inflates prevalence.

q: August intake is 111 cats, of which 6 arrive already infected. The resident census on August 1 is 39, of which 11 are infected and 3 recovered before August 1. How many cats are at risk?
e: Incoming animals at risk are 111 - 6 = 105, and resident animals at risk are 39 - 11 - 3 = 25, so 130 in total.

q: Which statement is correct about ratios, proportions and rates?
o: A rate incorporates the passage of time, and a male-to-female intake ratio is a ratio but not a proportion.
A rate is always greater than 1, and cumulative incidence is a ratio but not a proportion.
A rate has no denominator, and case fatality rate is a ratio but not a proportion.
e: A proportion has a numerator that is a subset of the denominator. A sex ratio compares two independent groups. A rate measures events per unit of time.

q: In a shelter intake ward, 40 unvaccinated dogs are housed and none show signs. Over the next 7 days, 12 develop confirmed parvovirus and 2 of the 12 die. What is the attack rate?
e: Attack rate is cumulative incidence over the outbreak window: 12 new cases divided by 40 at-risk dogs is 30%. 16.7% is the case fatality rate (2 of 12).

q: A cat colony has 200 cats at the start of the month, all free of ringworm. Over 30 days, 10 of these cats are newly diagnosed. Separately, 3 more cats arrive already infected and go straight to isolation. What is the cumulative incidence of ringworm for the month?
e: The at-risk denominator excludes animals infected on arrival, so cumulative incidence is 10 new cases divided by 200 at-risk cats, which is 5%.

q: A cat room is monitored for feline URI over 2 weeks. Summed across all cats, the room logs 500 cat-days at risk, and 10 cats develop new URI signs. What is the incidence rate per 100 cat-days?
o: 20 cases per 100 cat-days
0.2 cases per 100 cat-days
2 cases per 100 cat-days
e: Incidence rate is 10 divided by 500 cat-days, multiplied by 100, which is 2 cases per 100 cat-days.

q: On one day, a shelter tests all 80 cats in the building for FeLV, and 6 are positive. What is the point prevalence?
e: Point prevalence is existing cases at one instant: 6 divided by 80 is 7.5%.

q: In one month, 25 dogs in a ward have signs of kennel cough at some point: 15 already had signs at the start, and 10 developed new signs. The average daily population is 100. What is the period prevalence?
e: Period prevalence counts all cases, existing plus new, present at any time in the interval: 25 divided by 100 is 25%. The 10% figure is the cumulative incidence.

q: How is relative risk calculated in a cohort study, and when does the odds ratio from a case-control study approximate it?
o: The odds of exposure in cases divided by controls; when exposure is rare
Incidence in the exposed divided by incidence in the unexposed; when the disease is rare
Deaths divided by confirmed cases; when the study is prospective
e: Relative risk is the ratio of incidence in exposed to unexposed animals. Under the rare-disease assumption, the odds ratio approximates it.

q: How are ratio measures interpreted: a relative risk of 1.0, a relative risk of 0.6 for vaccinated animals, and an odds ratio with a 95% confidence interval that includes 1?
o: 1.0 is a doubling of risk, 0.6 is an increased risk, and an interval including 1 is significant
1.0 is no association, 0.6 is a protective effect, and an interval including 1 is not significant
1.0 is a strong protective effect, 0.6 is no association, and an interval including 0 is not significant
e: The null value for a ratio measure is 1, meaning no association. Below 1 indicates reduced risk, and an interval that includes 1 is not statistically significant.

q: Which measure gives the absolute excess risk in the exposed group compared with the unexposed group?
o: Attributable risk (risk difference)
Odds ratio
Relative risk
e: Attributable risk is the difference in incidence between exposed and unexposed groups, an absolute measure.

q: A 2x2 table shows exposed cases 40, exposed non-cases 60, unexposed cases 20 and unexposed non-cases 80. What is the relative risk?
e: Risk in the exposed is 40/100 = 0.4, and in the unexposed 20/100 = 0.2, so the relative risk is 0.4/0.2 = 2.0.

q: In a shelter trial, URI incidence is 30% in unvaccinated cats and 10% in vaccinated cats. What is the number needed to treat, and from which statistic is it derived?
o: 5, derived from the absolute risk reduction
3, derived from the relative risk
10, derived from the odds ratio
e: The absolute risk reduction is 30% - 10% = 0.20, and NNT = 1 / 0.20 = 5. Five cats must be vaccinated to prevent one case.

q: Ten dogs are confirmed with parvovirus and four die. What is the case fatality rate, and how does it differ from a mortality rate?
o: 40%; its denominator is confirmed cases, whereas a mortality rate uses the whole population
4%; its denominator is the whole population, whereas a mortality rate uses cases
25%; it measures incidence, whereas a mortality rate measures prevalence
e: Case fatality rate is deaths divided by confirmed cases (4/10 = 40%) and reflects severity. Mortality rates use the whole population as the denominator.

q: Which measure is the proportion of the whole shelter population that dies from any cause in a period?
o: The case fatality rate
The crude (all-cause) mortality rate
The attack rate
e: Crude mortality uses the whole at-risk population as the denominator and includes deaths from all causes.

q: Over 3 months, a shelter's average population is 150 animals. Twenty-two are confirmed with distemper, and 6 die. What is the cause-specific mortality rate for distemper?
e: Cause-specific mortality uses the whole population at risk: 6 divided by 150 is 4%. The 27.3% figure (6/22) is the case fatality rate.

q: Morbidity in a population is best described by which measure?
o: The death rate
The case fatality rate
The incidence or prevalence of illness
e: Morbidity refers to the occurrence of illness, captured by incidence or prevalence.

q: A shelter deliberately seeks out cases rather than waiting for them to be reported. Which type of surveillance is this?
o: Active surveillance
Passive surveillance
Sentinel reporting
e: Active surveillance involves deliberately seeking cases, whereas passive surveillance relies on cases being reported.

q: In the population approach to disease, what is the equivalent of forming a differential diagnosis for an individual?
o: Performing a physical examination on each animal
Recording an individual history for each animal
Formulating epidemiological hypotheses about the frequency and distribution of disease
e: At the population level, the clinician forms hypotheses to explain the observed frequency and distribution of disease.

q: Which statements are correct: a disease at its usual expected baseline is endemic, R0 assumes a wholly susceptible population, and which reproduction number changes during an outbreak?
o: Epidemic; R0 falls as vaccination coverage rises; R0 changes
Sporadic; R0 is the incubation period of the pathogen; neither R0 nor R changes
Endemic; R0 is the expected number of secondary cases from one case in a wholly susceptible population; the effective reproduction number R changes
e: Endemic is the expected baseline. R0 is a fixed property of the pathogen and setting, whereas the effective reproduction number R reflects the currently susceptible population and moves as immunity and control measures accumulate.

q: Which epidemic curve pattern matches its source?
o: A single sharp peak suggests a propagated outbreak, and waves spaced by the incubation period suggest a point source.
A single sharp peak suggests a point source, waves spaced by the incubation period suggest a propagated outbreak, and a broad plateau suggests a continuous source.
A broad plateau suggests a point source, and irregular clusters suggest a propagated outbreak.
e: A point source gives one sharp peak within an incubation period, propagated spread gives successive waves spaced by the incubation period, continuous exposure gives a broad hump, and intermittent exposure gives irregular clusters.

q: What is the purpose of a case definition early in an outbreak investigation, and what three components is it built from?
o: To assign blame for the outbreak; incidence, prevalence and mortality
To replace diagnostic testing; sensitivity, specificity and prevalence
To count cases consistently; person, place and time
e: A standard case definition lets investigators count cases consistently. It is built from person (vulnerability), place (facility boundaries) and time (relevant period).

q: Attack rates calculated for different subgroups during an outbreak are used mainly to
o: measure long-term prevalence.
identify which groups are at highest risk.
estimate length of stay.
e: Comparing attack rates across subgroups highlights the highest-risk groups and points toward the source.

q: The sensitivity of a surveillance system refers to
o: how quickly it reports.
the proportion of true cases that it detects.
its running cost.
e: Surveillance sensitivity is the proportion of actual cases that the system successfully detects.

q: Which stage of disease occurs before any pathological change, when host, agent and environment interact to establish susceptibility?
o: The prepathogenesis period
The pathogenesis period
The incubation period
e: The prepathogenesis period precedes the onset of pathological change. The pathogenesis period begins once those changes start.

q: In the CDC field-epidemiology framework for outbreak investigation, which step comes immediately before developing and testing hypotheses?
o: Implementing control measures
Communicating the findings
Applying descriptive epidemiology by person, place and time
e: The sequence runs: confirm the outbreak, verify the diagnosis, define cases, find cases, apply descriptive epidemiology, and then develop and test hypotheses.
